title: Watermarking Without Standards Is Not AI Governance
claim: Enforceable governance needs stacked layers of technical requirements, audit infrastructure, and policy enforcement, a structure mature regulated domains already use.
layout: 2 stacked parts: precedent table on top, pyramid with right-pointing mechanism boxes below
description: The figure has two parts. The top is a table with three rows (Layer 1: Technical requirements, Layer 2: Audit infrastructure, Layer 3: Policy and enforcement). It has three columns of regulatory precedent: cryptographic modules (NIST CMVP), medical devices (FDA), and AI systems (EU AI Act). The cells name the relevant standards, accredited labs or notified bodies, and market gating or penalties. The bottom is a three-tier pyramid in graded purple shades, darkest at the top (Layer 3) and lightest at the base (Layer 1). Each tier has a black arrow pointing right to a rounded box with three bullets of concrete mechanisms, such as shared perturbation benchmarks, cryptographic commitments, and enforced penalties. On the left, a solid curved arrow labeled evidence runs upward and a dashed curved arrow labeled revision runs downward. The eye goes first to the pyramid.
caption: A three-layer framework for enforceable watermarking. Each layer represents a distinct governance function: technical guarantees, independent auditability, and regulatory enforcement. Arrows to the right point to concrete mechanisms that instantiate the requirements at each level, linking system design to policy accountability. Arrows to the left show the feedback between layers, with evidence flowing upward and revision flowing back down.
abstract: Watermarking has emerged as a leading technical proposal for attributing generative AI content and is increasingly cited in global governance frameworks. This position paper argues that current implementations risk serving as symbolic compliance rather than delivering effective oversight. We identify a growing gap between regulatory expectations and the technical limitations of existing watermarking schemes. Through analysis of policy proposals and industry practices, we show how incentive structures disincentivize robust, auditable deployments. To realign watermarking with governance goals, we propose a three-layer framework encompassing technical standards, audit infrastructure, and enforcement mechanisms. Without enforceable requirements and independent verification, watermarking will remain inadequate for accountability and ultimately undermine broader efforts in AI safety and regulation.
